readings.title: Lecture XXII, §1
readings.text: 1. Even of itself the teaching of the Blessed Paul is sufficient to give you a full assurance concerning those Divine Mysteries, of which having been deemed worthy, ye are become of the same body and blood with Christ. For you have just heard him say distinctly, That our Lord Jesus Christ in the night in which He was betrayed, took bread, and when He had given thanks He brake it, and gave to His disciples, saying, Take, eat, this is My Body: and having taken the cup and given thanks, He said, Take, drink, this is My Blood . Since then He Himself declared and said of the Bread, This is My Body, who shall dare to doubt any longer? And since He has Himself affirmed and said, This is My Blood, who shall ever hesitate, saying, that it is not His blood?

readings.title: Lecture XXII, §2
readings.text: 2. He once in Cana of Galilee, turned the water into wine, akin to blood , and is it incredible that He should have turned wine into blood? When called to a bodily marriage, He miraculously wrought that wonderful work; and on the children of the bride-chamber , shall He not much rather be acknowledged to have bestowed the fruition of His Body and Blood ?

readings.title: Lecture XXII, §3
readings.text: 3. Wherefore with full assurance let us partake as of the Body and Blood of Christ: for in the figure of Bread is given to thee His Body, and in the figure of Wine His Blood; that thou by partaking of the Body and Blood of Christ, mayest be made of the same body and the same blood with Him. For thus we come to bear Christ in us, because His Body and Blood are distributed through our members; thus it is that, according to the blessed Peter, we become partakers of the divine nature .

readings.title: Lecture XXII, §4
readings.text: 4. Christ on a certain occasion discoursing with the Jews said, Except ye eat My flesh and drink My blood, ye have no life in you . They not having heard His saying in a spiritual sense were offended, and went back, supposing that He was inviting them to eat flesh.

readings.title: Lecture XXII, §5
readings.text: 5. In the Old Testament also there was shew-bread; but this, as it belonged to the Old Testament, has come to an end; but in the New Testament there is Bread of heaven, and a Cup of salvation, sanctifying soul and body; for as the Bread corresponds to our body, so is the Word appropriate to our soul.

readings.title: Lecture XXII, §6
readings.text: 6. Consider therefore the Bread and the Wine not as bare elements, for they are, according to the Lord's declaration, the Body and Blood of Christ; for even though sense suggests this to thee, yet let faith establish thee. Judge not the matter from the taste, but from faith be fully assured without misgiving, that the Body and Blood of Christ have been vouchsafed to thee.

readings.title: Lecture XXII, §7
readings.text: 7. Also the blessed David shall advise thee the meaning of this, saying, Thou hast prepared a table before me in the presence of them that afflict me . What he says, is to this effect: Before Thy coming, the evil spirits prepared a table for men , polluted and defiled and full of devilish influence ; but since Thy coming. O Lord, Thou hast prepared a table before me. When the man says to God, Thou hast prepared before me a table, what other does he indicate but that mystical and spiritual Table, which God hath prepared for us over against, that is, contrary and in opposition to the evil spirits? And very truly; for that had communion with devils, but this, with God. Thou hast anointed my head with oil . With oil He anointed thine head upon thy forehead, for the seal which thou hast of God; that thou mayest be made the engraving of the signet, Holiness unto God . And thy cup intoxicateth me, as very strong . Thou seest that cup here spoken of, which Jesus took in His hands, and gave thanks, and said, This is My blood, which is shed for many for the remission of sins .

readings.title: Lecture XXII, §8
readings.text: 8. Therefore Solomon also, hinting at this grace, says in Ecclesiastes, Come hither, eat thy bread with joy (that is, the spiritual bread; Come hither, he calls with the call to salvation and blessing), and drink thy wine with a merry heart (that is, the spiritual wine); and let oil be poured out upon thy head (thou seest he alludes even to the mystic Chrism); and let thy garments be always white, for the Lord is well pleased with thy works ; for before thou camest to Baptism, thy works were vanity of vanities . But now, having put off thy old garments, and put on those which are spiritually white, thou must be continually robed in white: of course we mean not this, that thou art always to wear white raiment; but thou must be clad in the garments that are truly white and shining and spiritual, that thou mayest say with the blessed Esaias, My soul shall be joyful in my God; for He hath clothed me with a garment of salvation, and put a robe of gladness around me .

readings.title: Lecture XXII, §9
readings.text: 9. Having learnt these things, and been fully assured that the seeming bread is not bread, though sensible to taste, but the Body of Christ; and that the seeming wine is not wine, though the taste will have it so, but the Blood of Christ ; and that of this David sung of old, saying, And bread strengtheneth man's heart, to make his face to shine with oil , "strengthen thou thine heart," by partaking thereof as spiritual, and "make the face of thy soul to shine." And so having it unveiled with a pure conscience, mayest thou reflect as a mirror the glory of the Lord , and proceed from glory to glory, in Christ Jesus our Lord:--To whom be honour, and might, and glory, for ever and ever. Amen.

scripture.translation: King James Version (public domain in the United States)
scripture.text:
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life.

I am that bread of life.

Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.

This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die.

I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.

The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying, How can this man give us his flesh to eat?

Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.

Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.

For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.

He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him.

As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me.

This is that bread which came down from heaven: not as your fathers did eat manna, and are dead: he that eateth of this bread shall live for ever.

overview.text: Cyril explains the Eucharist to newly initiated Christians through Christ’s words and the testimony of Scripture. Eucharistic gifts means the bread and wine received in this sacrament. His central distinction is between what the senses perceive and what Christ declares the gifts to be.
overview.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: What is the foundation of Cyril’s teaching?

paragraphs.text: Cyril begins with Paul’s account of Christ giving bread and the cup to his disciples. He grounds confidence about the sacrament in Christ’s identification of them as his body and blood. His reasoning rests on the speaker’s authority.

paragraphs.text: The change of water into wine at Cana supplies an example of Christ’s power. Cyril uses it to argue that a change associated with the Eucharistic cup should not be dismissed as impossible. The wedding miracle functions as an analogy within his argument.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: What participation does the sacrament give?

paragraphs.text: Cyril describes receiving Christ’s body and blood under the forms of bread and wine. He connects this participation with bearing Christ and sharing in divine life. His account concerns communion with Christ, rather than ordinary bodily nourishment alone.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: How does he distinguish this from ordinary eating?

paragraphs.text: Cyril recalls hearers who understood Christ’s language about eating his flesh in a merely bodily way and were offended. His explanation calls for a spiritual understanding. Within this lecture, spiritual does not mean that the gifts are only imaginary or mere reminders.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: How does Cyril relate the two Testaments?

paragraphs.text: Cyril contrasts the Old Testament showbread with the bread and cup of the New Testament. He describes the latter as sanctifying body and soul. The comparison places the Eucharist within his account of scriptural fulfillment.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: Why does he distinguish faith from taste?

paragraphs.text: Cyril observes that the senses encounter the appearances of bread and wine. He nevertheless identifies the gifts according to Christ’s declaration. His argument makes faith in those words decisive for understanding the sacrament.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: How does he interpret the table and cup in the Psalms?

paragraphs.text: Cyril reads the prepared table, anointing, and cup as images connected with Christian initiation and communion. He contrasts communion with God with the rival worship described in his passage. This is his sacramental interpretation of the Psalm’s language.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: What do the white garments signify?

paragraphs.text: Cyril connects bread, wine, oil, and white clothing in his interpretation of Ecclesiastes. He explicitly explains spiritual white garments through the renewed life, rather than requiring permanently white clothing. The image concerns the meaning of the recipient’s baptismal change.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: How does Cyril conclude his account of the gifts?

paragraphs.text: Cyril restates that the sensible appearances do not exhaust the gifts’ identity as Christ’s body and blood. He connects receiving them with spiritual strengthening and the transformation of the person. The concluding praise belongs to the original lecture.
